meta.title: Marvel Reading Guide 2000-Now
meta.notes: Order = rotated backbone reading order (arc-sized chunks, Planet X-style). Links verified against the marvelcomicsapp.com API; see status per collection.

eras.name: New Marvel / Planet X to Decimation
eras.blurb: The modern Marvel voice arrives: Morrison's X-Men, Bendis's Daredevil and Avengers, JMS's Spider-Man, the Ultimate line in parallel - ending in House of M and Decimation.
eras.skipped: Filler and mediocre tie-ins were cut per this era's Notable Skips research (see the era files in the research archive); every event's buildup, core and fallout is kept.

eras.name: Civil War to Avengers vs. X-Men
eras.blurb: The Bendis event era: Civil War, Secret Invasion, Dark Reign, the Messiah Trilogy, DnA cosmic, Brubaker's Captain America and Hickman's Fantastic Four - converging on Avengers vs. X-Men.
eras.skipped: Filler and mediocre tie-ins were cut per this era's Notable Skips research (see the era files in the research archive); every event's buildup, core and fallout is kept.
eras.footnote: Disclosure (Era 03 §4.2 / TB-3): Marvel's official 2008 checklist interleaves the New Avengers / Mighty Avengers flashback issues by release order. This guide deliberately reads them as reveal-gated blocks instead (Veranke block after SI #3/#4; Pym block after SI #6), per Bendis's flashback design, to protect the event's two biggest reveals. The blocks are a stated spoiler-protection choice - not the published consensus order.

eras.name: Marvel NOW / The Hickman Saga to Secret Wars
eras.blurb: Hickman's Avengers/New Avengers interleave is the spine: everything dies, Infinity burns, Time Runs Out, and Secret Wars ends the multiverse - with Aaron's Thor, Waid's Daredevil and the era's solo runs around it.
eras.skipped: Filler and mediocre tie-ins were cut per this era's Notable Skips research (see the era files in the research archive); every event's buildup, core and fallout is kept.

eras.name: Post-Secret Wars to House of X
eras.blurb: A rebuilt universe: Jane Foster's Thor, Secret Empire, Immortal Hulk, Aaron's Avengers and the road to House of X / Powers of X, which reboot the X-Men wholesale.
eras.skipped: Filler and mediocre tie-ins were cut per this era's Notable Skips research (see the era files in the research archive); every event's buildup, core and fallout is kept.

eras.name: Krakoa, Fall of X, and the Doom Era
eras.blurb: The Krakoan age in full - Dawn, Reign, Destiny, Fall - plus King in Black, Devil's Reign, Blood Hunt and One World Under Doom, and the new Ultimate Universe running alongside.
eras.skipped: Filler and mediocre tie-ins were cut per this era's Notable Skips research (see the era files in the research archive); every event's buildup, core and fallout is kept.

Resolution already exists (series 2570, verified in era-04-resolved.json) - this supplement is the missing extraction half. Hand-extracted supplement (M39(d)): extraction/era-04.json had zero mentions, so the build dropped the resolved record.

collections.why: Sins of Sinister strict order step 2 of 12 (Era 06 S A9, MUST-READ EVENT, architect Kieron Gillen). The alpha issue: Sinister assassinates the Council's hopes and corrupts resurrection with his own DNA; the timeline jumps. Step 1 (the on-ramp, Immortal X-Men #9-10) is already covered by the extraction entry Immortal X-Men (2022) #8-10 upstream - do not re-read. Hand-extracted supplement (Checker B Sweep 12): extraction emitted no Sins of Sinister entries at all.

Sins of Sinister strict order step 3 of 12 (Era 06 S A9). +10 years. X-Men Red becomes Storm & the Brotherhood of Mutants for the event: an elderly Storm leads Arakko's last mutants - the research calls Storm's thread the emotional core of the event.
Sins of Sinister strict order step 4 of 12 (Era 06 S A9). +10 years. Legion of X becomes Nightcrawlers: Spurrier's faith/horror thread inside Sinister's corrupted timeline.
Sins of Sinister strict order step 5 of 12 (Era 06 S A9). +10 years. Immortal X-Men becomes Immoral X-Men: Gillen's Quiet Council farce-to-horror under Sinister's corruption.
Sins of Sinister strict order step 6 of 12 (Era 06 S A9). +100 years. Spurrier's faith/horror thread deepens as the timeline degrades.
Sins of Sinister strict order step 7 of 12 (Era 06 S A9). +100 years. The corrupted Council a century into Sinister's win.
Sins of Sinister strict order step 8 of 12 (Era 06 S A9). +100 years. Storm's Brotherhood a century on - the event's emotional core continues.
Sins of Sinister strict order step 9 of 12 (Era 06 S A9). +1,000 years. The Council thread at the timeline's far end.
Sins of Sinister strict order step 10 of 12 (Era 06 S A9). +1,000 years. Storm's last stand at the end of Sinister's thousand-year timeline.
Sins of Sinister strict order step 11 of 12 (Era 06 S A9). +1,000 years. Spurrier's thread closes at the timeline's end.

Sins of Sinister strict order step 12 of 12 (Era 06 S A9). The omega issue: Mother Righteous' gambit; the timeline is reset via a Moira clone - but Sinister's corruption of the resurrection data survives the reset, and the Council now knows what he did. Resurrection is suspect from here into Fall of X.

primers.name: The Inhumans — Black Bolt & Medusa
primers.text: A hidden royal civilization of superhumans created by alien Kree experiments millennia ago, living in Attilan, isolated from humanity. Their powers come from Terrigen Mist exposure. King Black Bolt's voice can shatter mountains, so he rules in silence; Queen Medusa — whose hair moves with superhuman strength — speaks for him. Watch how this proud, insular monarchy handles contact with the outside world: that tension between isolation and intervention never goes away, and the Inhumans keep colliding with Earth's heroes for decades.

primers.name: Daredevil — Matt Murdock
primers.text: A blind Hell's Kitchen lawyer whose other senses are superhumanly sharp — he "sees" via a radar-like perception of sound, heartbeat, and motion. By night he's Daredevil, an acrobatic, billy-club-swinging vigilante driven by Catholic guilt and a refusal to let his neighborhood's predators win. Matt's tragedy engine is that his two lives constantly destroy each other: every secret identity has a cost, and everyone close to him pays it. This era will test him harder than any hero in the guide.

primers.name: The Punisher — Frank Castle
primers.text: A decorated Marine whose wife and children were murdered in a mob crossfire. Frank Castle responded by declaring a one-man war on crime — no arrests, no rehabilitation, just military-grade lethality applied with tactical precision. He has no powers; his "ability" is preparation, pain tolerance, and absolute certainty. Other heroes tolerate him at best. Watch how the guide uses him as a measuring stick: whenever Castle appears, the story is asking where the line between justice and murder actually sits.

primers.name: The Sentry — Robert Reynolds
primers.text: A forgotten hero. Bob Reynolds was supposedly a Superman-level Marvel hero from the very beginning — "the power of a million exploding suns" — whom the entire world, including himself, somehow forgot. His re-emergence is framed as a mystery: why was he erased? The Sentry introduces a pattern this era loves — immense power paired with a fragile mind. Treat him as a loaded gun placed on the Avengers' table early; the guide will keep coming back to him at the worst possible moments.

primers.name: Marvel Boy — Noh-Varr
primers.text: A young Kree soldier from an alternate-timeline empire, crash-landed on Earth with his crew dead and a head full of propaganda. Genetically engineered with insect DNA, he's super-strong, can reroute his nervous system, and is furiously contemptuous of humanity — he arrives essentially as a teenage terrorist with a manifesto. Watch him closely anyway: the guide plants him early because the question of whether Earth can turn this angry alien kid into something else runs, quietly, for twenty years.

primers.name: Black Panther — T'Challa
primers.text: King of Wakanda, the most technologically advanced nation on Earth, hidden in Africa and rich beyond measure from vibranium — the metal that absorbs vibration and powers Wakandan science. T'Challa is a warrior-king, a genius inventor, and a master strategist who treats superheroics as statecraft: every alliance is also diplomacy. He is never merely a team member. Watch how often his first loyalty — Wakanda — puts him at odds with friends, and how rarely he explains himself before acting.

primers.name: Spider-Man — Peter Parker
primers.text: You know the basics: bitten by a radioactive spider, learned that with great power comes great responsibility the hardest way. At this point in continuity Peter is a married schoolteacher, broke as ever, and about to have his understanding of his own powers upended — new questions arise about whether the spider chose him and what else shares that connection. This era is unusually cruel to Peter. Watch his marriage, his secret identity, and his place among the Avengers: all three become battlegrounds.

primers.name: Jessica Jones
primers.text: A former superhero who quit. Jessica gained super-strength and limited flight in the same accident that killed her family, tried the hero life, and walked away after trauma the series reveals slowly. Now she's a hard-drinking private investigator in Hell's Kitchen taking the cases nobody glamorous touches. *Alias* is the guide's ground floor — the Marvel Universe seen from a bar stool. Jessica's importance grows far beyond her own series; her detective's eye for damaged people makes her a connective thread everywhere.

primers.name: Wolverine — Logan
primers.text: The X-Men's feral berserker: healing factor, adamantium-laced skeleton, three claws per hand, senses like a wolf — and, for a century of publication, no past. Weapon X stole his memories; even his name was a fragment. *Origin* finally shows his nineteenth-century beginnings, and the guide places it here so everything after carries that weight. Logan is the X-line's moral weather vane: killer trying to be a man, teacher of kids he pretends not to care about. Nearly every X-event turns on what Logan chooses.

primers.name: Professor X — Charles Xavier
primers.text: The world's most powerful telepath and founder of the X-Men, preaching coexistence between mutants and humans from his Westchester school. But read him carefully from the start of this era: Xavier's dream has always required secrets, compromises, and occasional ruthless telepathic interventions that his students never consented to. Morrison's run opens with him more public and confident than ever — a mutant celebrity. The guide's long arc asks whether the dream was ever as clean as he sold it. Nobody's reputation changes more across these 26 years.

primers.name: Magneto — Erik Lehnsherr
primers.text: Holocaust survivor, master of magnetism, and Xavier's oldest friend and ideological opposite: where Charles preaches integration, Erik believes mutants must dominate or be exterminated — because he has seen exactly how humanity treats the powerless. At this era's start he is presumed dead after the destruction of the mutant nation Genosha, which hangs over everything. Magneto is never simply a villain in this guide; he is the argument the X-Men can never fully refute. Watch every appearance: his shadow shapes mutant politics even in absence.

primers.name: Emma Frost
primers.text: A diamond-hard telepath — literally: she can shift into an organic diamond form, trading her psychic powers for near-invulnerability. Emma began as the White Queen of the villainous Hellfire Club, a woman who weaponized wealth, sex, and other people's secrets. By this era she's defected to the X-Men as a teacher, and nobody — students, teammates, readers — is sure the conversion is real. Her acid wit hides the era's most guarded heart. Emma becomes one of the defining X-Men of the next two decades; watch her rise.

primers.name: Jean Grey — Phoenix
primers.text: The X-Men's heart: an omega-level telepath and telekinetic who once hosted the Phoenix Force, a cosmic entity of life, death, and rebirth that amplified her power to godlike levels — and has never entirely left her story. Jean is married to Scott Summers, anchors the school's moral center, and is the person everyone trusts most. Which is precisely why Morrison's run keeps placing her at the center of its storms. In this universe, "Phoenix" is never just a codename. Remember what the fire means whenever it flickers.

primers.name: Cyclops — Scott Summers
primers.text: The X-Men's field leader since he was a teenager, firing uncontrollable optic blasts he keeps in check with a ruby-quartz visor. Scott is the soldier Xavier made: disciplined, repressed, brilliant at tactics, terrible at having a life. Morrison's era finds his marriage strained and his faith in the dream quietly cracking — he starts asking what the X-Men are *for* if the dream never arrives. Follow Scott above almost anyone: his radicalization arc across this guide is one of its central through-lines, from boy scout to something far more complicated.

primers.name: Cassandra Nova
primers.text: The first villain of the modern era, and one of the worst. Cassandra Nova is Xavier's dark mirror — a psychic entity of immense power and pure, patient malice, introduced as she orchestrates an atrocity against mutantkind using hijacked Sentinel technology. She doesn't want money or territory; she wants to unmake everything Charles Xavier has built, personally. Her opening move sets the body count and the tone for the entire X-line going forward. When later stories speak of mutantkind's trauma and paranoia, it starts here, with her.

primers.name: Xorn
primers.text: A new teacher at Xavier's school: a Chinese mutant prisoner rescued by the X-Men, wearing an iron mask that contains the star burning where his brain should be. Xorn is gentle, philosophical, a healer whose energy can mend others — the calm center of Morrison's chaotic school. Students adore him. That's all you should know, and it's genuinely all the characters know. Morrison's run is famous for its endgame twists; simply enjoy Xorn as the run presents him, and let the story do what it does. No further questions.

primers.name: The Fantastic Four — Reed Richards & Family
primers.text: Marvel's First Family: Reed Richards (Mr. Fantastic), the smartest man alive, who stretches and invents; Sue Storm, the Invisible Woman, the team's actual spine; Johnny Storm, the Human Torch; Ben Grimm, the ever-lovin' Thing. They're explorers first and superheroes second — a family that argues at the dinner table and then saves the universe. Reed is the key figure: his genius, arrogance, and habit of deciding things *for* everyone quietly drive half the events in this guide. Never ignore what Reed is building.

primers.name: Doctor Doom — Victor von Doom
primers.text: Monarch of Latveria, master of both science and sorcery, encased in armor of his own design, face scarred by an accident he blames on Reed Richards. Doom is Marvel's greatest villain because he is frequently *right* — his nation prospers, his will is absolute, and his code of honor is real, if monstrous. He considers himself humanity's only fit ruler. Keep this primer in mind for 26 years: Doom's ambition escalates in stages across the whole guide, and every stage makes a twisted kind of sense from where he stands.

primers.name: The Runaways
primers.text: Six Los Angeles teenagers who discover their parents are secretly a cabal of supervillains called the Pride — mobsters, mutants, aliens, time-travelers, and dark wizards who run the city's underworld. The kids do the only sensible thing: they run. Armed with stolen heirlooms (a staff, a gauntlet, a telepathic dinosaur), they try to survive and undo their parents' plans. The Runaways matter because they're the guide's purest found-family story, and because these kids keep resurfacing in the wider universe as adults who never stopped running.

primers.name: Scarlet Witch — Wanda Maximoff
primers.text: An Avenger whose "hex" powers evolved into full reality-warping chaos magic — she can rewrite probability, matter, and eventually reality itself, and her control has never matched her power. Wanda's history is a pile of tragedies: lost children who may never have been real, a husband (the Vision) whose love ended in erasure, manipulations by demons and Doom alike. As *Disassembled* opens, something is very wrong with her. Wanda is the single most consequential person in this era — treat every appearance as an earthquake warning.

primers.name: Hawkeye — Clint Barton
primers.text: The Avengers' resident normal person: a carny-trained archer with trick arrows, a big mouth, and no powers whatsoever, standing next to gods and supersoldiers through sheer nerve. Clint is the team's blue-collar conscience — the one who says what everyone's thinking and charges in anyway. *Disassembled* hits him personally and hard; remember where he stands when the dust settles. His arc across this guide — Avenger, casualty of chaos, and eventually the star of one of its most beloved street-level runs — is a quiet spine of the whole project.

primers.name: Nick Fury & S.H.I.E.L.D.
primers.text: Fury is the world's spymaster: a WWII soldier kept vital by the Infinity Formula, director of S.H.I.E.L.D., the global intelligence agency that monitors superhuman threats. Fury operates on a simple creed — the ends justify almost anything, and heroes are assets. *Secret War* shows what that creed costs when he acts on it without telling anyone. S.H.I.E.L.D. itself is a permanent institution of this era: part shield, part surveillance state. Watch the trust between Fury, his agency, and the hero community — it is already cracking.

primers.name: Captain America — Steve Rogers
primers.text: A frail kid from Brooklyn given the Super-Soldier Serum in WWII, frozen in ice, and revived into a century he doesn't recognize. Steve Rogers is the moral center of the Marvel Universe — not because he's the strongest, but because everyone, friend and enemy, measures themselves against him. Brubaker's run, where this primer anchors, drags his wartime past into the present with a conspiracy's patience. Everything in this era — Civil War, Dark Reign, Siege — is ultimately about who gets to claim what Steve Rogers stands for.

primers.name: The Winter Soldier
primers.text: A ghost from the Cold War: a Soviet assassin kept in cryogenic storage between missions, woken to kill, wiped, and frozen again for decades — a rumor intelligence agencies barely believe. He surfaces in Brubaker's run working for a former Soviet general with a stolen Cosmic Cube, and his trail leads straight into the deepest wound of Steve Rogers' past. That's all you get; this is one of the great reveals of the era, and the run earns it. Just watch Steve's face when the pieces start fitting together.

primers.name: Iron Man — Tony Stark
primers.text: Billionaire engineer who built a suit of armor to escape captivity and became Iron Man. Tony's defining trait isn't genius — it's control: he believes every problem, including superheroes themselves, can be engineered into safety. *Extremis* upgrades his body into the machine, literally wiring the armor into his nervous system, and it's a perfect symbol of where he's heading. Tony is the co-protagonist of this entire era alongside Steve Rogers, and their collision over what heroes owe the world drives the decade. Watch his certainty. It's his superpower and his flaw.

primers.name: The Young Avengers
primers.text: In the wreckage of *Disassembled*, with the Avengers disbanded, a group of teenagers independently takes up the mantle: Patriot, Hulkling, Wiccan, Speed, a young Hawkeye named Kate Bishop, and others — each connected to the Avengers' legacy in ways that unfold slowly. They're not sidekicks; nobody asked them, and the adult heroes mostly want them to stop. This team matters enormously out of proportion to its page count: several of Marvel's most important next-generation figures debut here, including two young men whose heritage reshapes cosmic and magical corners of the universe.

primers.name: Kate Bishop — Hawkeye
primers.text: A wealthy Manhattan teenager who, after surviving a traumatic attack, trained herself relentlessly in archery, fencing, and martial arts so she'd never be helpless again — then talked her way onto the Young Avengers and claimed the Hawkeye name while Clint Barton was gone. Kate has no powers, just money, skill, and refusal. She's the clearest example of this era's generational handoff: the legacy heroes aren't coming to save the future, so the kids seize the names themselves. Her later solo spotlight is one of the guide's highlights.

primers.name: Kingpin — Wilson Fisk
primers.text: New York's emperor of crime: a mountain of a man whose bulk is muscle, whose empire is built on patience, information, and perfectly deniable violence. Fisk doesn't rage — he acquires. Bendis's *Daredevil* run, where he looms largest in this era's opening, is essentially a war between Fisk and Matt Murdock for the soul of Hell's Kitchen, fought through lawyers, leaks, and blood. Fisk's ambitions don't stay street-level forever. A man who can run a city's underworld this well will eventually wonder what else he could run. ---

primers.name: Quicksilver — Pietro Maximoff
primers.text: Wanda's twin brother, a speedster whose impatience is a personality and a tragedy. After House of M ends, Pietro wakes powerless — and for a man whose entire identity was motion and mutant pride, that's a death sentence he refuses to accept. *Son of M* follows his desperate attempt to restore what was lost, whatever it costs whoever's nearby. Pietro is the Decimation era's cautionary tale: grief plus speed plus terrible judgment. His choices in this stretch echo into Inhuman and mutant politics for years.

primers.name: Decimation & The 198 — CONCEPT
primers.text: After House of M, the mutant population collapses overnight from millions to roughly 198 powered individuals — "M-Day." No new mutants are being born; the species is one bad winter from extinction. The remaining mutants cluster at Xavier's school under government "protection" that looks increasingly like internment, watched by Sentinel guards. Everything in the X-line for the next seven years flows from this number: every strategy, schism, and desperate gamble is about a species counting its own survivors. When characters say "the 198," they mean the whole endangered world.

primers.name: X-Factor Investigations — Jamie Madrox & Team
primers.text: Jamie Madrox, the Multiple Man, creates duplicates of himself with a kinetic impact — and each dupe has its own personality, skills, and opinions, which he reabsorbs (usually). After Decimation he reopens X-Factor as a mutant detective agency in crumbling Mutant Town: noir cases, missing persons, and the street-level reality of a dying species, staffed by misfits like Strong Guy, Wolfsbane, and the precognitive Layla Miller — a teenager who unsettlingly "knows stuff." This book is the X-line's conscience at ground level while the flagships fight wars.

primers.name: The Illuminati — CONCEPT / TEAM
primers.text: A secret council of the Marvel Universe's most powerful minds, formed years ago and revealed here: Iron Man, Reed Richards, Professor X, Doctor Strange, Black Bolt, and Namor — each representing a power bloc (science, magic, mutants, Inhumans, Atlantis). They meet in shadows to manage threats too big or too dirty for public heroics, and they answer to no one. Almost every catastrophe of the next decade has an Illuminati decision buried in its foundations. When the guide says "the road to hell was paved by six men in a room," this is the room.

primers.name: Namor — The Sub-Mariner
primers.text: Marvel's oldest anti-hero: the half-human king of Atlantis, immensely strong, able to fly, and possessed of a temper that has flooded cities. Namor sits on the Illuminati as the ocean's representative, and his loyalty is always to Atlantis first — a fact the surface world keeps relearning painfully. He is arrogant, honorable, magnetic, and completely unbothered by human morality. Watch his alliances: Namor serves with heroes, mutants, and monsters across this guide, and each time, the deciding vote is what serves his kingdom and his pride.

primers.name: Doctor Strange — Stephen Strange
primers.text: Once the world's greatest neurosurgeon, now its Sorcerer Supreme: guardian of Earth's dimension against magical and extradimensional threats, operating from the Sanctum Sanctorum in Greenwich Village. Strange is the Illuminati's mystical seat and the Avengers' occult insurance policy. At this point he's at the height of his power and confidence — which makes him a man who keeps dangerous secrets professionally. Magic in this universe always has a price, and Strange has been deferring payments for years. The bill is a recurring plot point of the entire guide.

primers.name: The Hulk — Bruce Banner
primers.text: A gamma-powered Jekyll and Hyde: mild physicist Bruce Banner transforms under stress into the Hulk, the strongest creature on Earth, whose rage scales with his anger. The Illuminati decide he's too dangerous to keep on Earth — that decision launches *Planet Hulk*, where he's exiled to a savage world of gladiator arenas and becomes something nobody predicted: a king, a liberator, a husband. Banner's intellect and the Hulk's grievance are both real. When he eventually looks back toward Earth, remember exactly who put him on that rocket.

primers.name: Thanos — The Mad Titan
primers.text: A mutant-born Eternal of Titan, obsessed with Death — whom he courts as a literal lover — and with proving his devotion through mass murder on a cosmic scale. Thanos is brilliant, philosophical, and patient; he treats genocide as an argument. The guide meets him in a strange, reflective phase during the Annihilation era, which makes him more dangerous, not less: he's *thinking*. File him away as the cosmic line's gravitational center. Every few years, the entire universe's story bends around this one purple philosopher of extinction.

primers.name: Nova — Richard Rider
primers.text: The last of the Nova Corps. Rider was a Long Island teenager given a Nova Centurion's power — flight, strength, energy manipulation, and the Worldmind, the living Xandarian supercomputer that now lives in his head because Xandar itself is gone. *Annihilation* turns a B-list hero into the cosmic line's protagonist: a traumatized soldier holding a dead civilization's entire legacy in his skull. His growth across the cosmic saga — from rookie to the man empires call when the sky falls — is one of the guide's most satisfying long arcs.

primers.name: Annihilus & The Annihilation Wave — CONCEPT
primers.text: Annihilus rules the Negative Zone, a mirror universe of insects and entropy, sustained by the Cosmic Control Rod and an absolute terror of death. The Annihilation Wave is his invasion of our universe: a fleet beyond counting that doesn't conquer planets so much as consume them, harvesting worlds for resources. This is the event that drags Marvel's cosmic characters — long a neglected corner — into a genuine war story with real casualties. The Wave's arrival reorders cosmic politics for a decade: empires fall, and unlikely alliances (see Ronan, below) become necessary.

primers.name: Ronan the Accuser
primers.text: The Kree Empire's supreme public accuser: judge, jury, and executioner armed with the Universal Weapon, a hammer that reshapes matter and energy. Ronan begins as a rigid zealot of Kree law — the kind of man who'd prosecute his own side. The Annihilation War forces him into alliance with the very people his empire despises, and war reveals unexpected depth in the fanatic. He's a useful primer in this saga's central lesson: in Marvel Cosmic, today's implacable enemy is tomorrow's indispensable ally, and empires are just people under pressure.

primers.name: The Silver Surfer — Norrin Radd
primers.text: Herald of Galactus. Norrin Radd sacrificed his freedom to Galactus, the devourer of worlds, to spare his home planet Zenn-La — becoming a chrome-skinned, board-riding scout who finds worlds for his master to consume, and who famously rebelled to defend Earth. He wields the Power Cosmic: near-limitless energy manipulation at a terrible moral price. In the Annihilation era he's back in Galactus's shadow, and that servitude is one of the war's great wild cards. The Surfer embodies cosmic Marvel's favorite question: what does a good man owe a monster he serves?

primers.name: Galactus — CONCEPT / ENTITY
primers.text: A survivor of the universe before this one, reborn as a force of nature: a colossal being who must consume the life-energy of planets to live. Galactus is not evil — he's ecology, a predator above morality, served by heralds who scout his meals. That distinction matters enormously in the cosmic saga, where desperate powers repeatedly try to weaponize, capture, or bargain with him. Treat Galactus like weather with a will: you don't defeat him, you survive him, redirect him, or pay his price. Empires in this guide fall for forgetting that.

primers.name: Norman Osborn
primers.text: Industrialist, sociopath, and secretly the Green Goblin — Spider-Man's most personal enemy, a man who has made destroying Peter Parker a hobby between corporate takeovers. As *Civil War* reshapes the hero community, Osborn gets handed something unprecedented: legitimacy, as director of the Thunderbolts, the government's team of "reformed" villains hunting unregistered heroes. Osborn's genius is understanding that power in this new era wears a suit and holds a press conference. Watch him with both eyes. His ascent is the slow fuse under the entire Dark Reign period.

primers.name: Bucky Barnes — The Winter Soldier, Revealed
primers.text: By this point in the guide, the Winter Soldier's identity is known to the characters — and it changes everything about Steve Rogers' war. Bucky Barnes was Steve's teenage sidekick in WWII, presumed dead in the war's final days; instead he survived, maimed and amnesiac, to be rebuilt by the Soviets as their deniable assassin. Now free of his programming and drowning in guilt for decades of kills he barely remembers choosing, Bucky is the era's most damaged man with a gun. His road runs straight through the era's biggest Captain America stories.

primers.name: Hope Summers
primers.text: The first mutant born after M-Day — the first new mutant in a world where the species was sterilized overnight. Every faction in *Messiah Complex* reads her differently: savior, messiah, existential threat, weapon. She's an infant when the war over her begins, which is the point: Hope is a symbol before she's a person, and everyone wants to write her meaning. Cable's entire existence reorganizes around protecting her. As she grows up across the guide, watch the gap between what mutantkind needs her to be and who she actually is.

primers.name: Cable — Nathan Summers
primers.text: A soldier from a ruined future: the time-displaced son of Scott Summers, infected with a techno-organic virus he constantly holds at bay with his telekinesis, and raised as a weapon against Apocalypse. Cable's creed is prevention — he has seen futures so bad that present-day moral qualms look like luxuries. In the Messiah era he becomes something new: a father-protector running through time with an infant the whole world wants. Cable embodies the X-line's hardest question — how much of the present may you sacrifice to a future only you have seen?

primers.name: Bishop — Lucas Bishop
primers.text: A mutant lawman from a dystopian future where mutants were herded into camps — a future he believes began with Hope Summers. Bishop absorbs and redirects energy, carries a soldier's pragmatism, and has dedicated his life to preventing his timeline by any means necessary. In *Messiah Complex* that conviction makes him the X-Men's enemy from within their own extended family: a man hunting a baby because he's certain of what she becomes. Bishop is tragedy, not villainy — two survivors of two different apocalypses, both sure they're saving the world.

primers.name: The Skrulls — CONCEPT
primers.text: A shape-shifting alien empire, ancient enemies of the Kree, whose religious prophecy promises them Earth as a promised world. Modern Skrull infiltration is undetectable — sleeper agents who don't just imitate heroes' bodies but their memories and personalities, placed over years. *Secret Invasion* is built on the paranoia that revelation creates: anyone, at any point in stories you've already read, might have been replaced. The primer rule for the reader is the characters' rule: trust is now a resource, and it's spent. He loves you — that's what they say. Believe no one cheaply.

primers.name: Dark Reign — CONCEPT (Osborn's America)
primers.text: Not an event — a status quo. After Secret Invasion, Norman Osborn, live on camera, becomes the most trusted man in America and is handed the keys: he replaces S.H.I.E.L.D. with his own agency, H.A.M.M.E.R., staffs a "Dark" Avengers team of villains in heroes' costumes, and runs a shadow cabal with Loki, Doom, Emma Frost, Namor, and the Hood. For roughly a year of guide-time, the Marvel Universe is a place where the monster won the election and governs competently. Every hero book in this stretch is about living under that sky.

primers.name: Secret Warriors — Daisy Johnson & Nick Fury's Secret Team
primers.text: While the world thinks Nick Fury is finished, he's quietly building an army. His "caterpillars" are young, off-the-books superhumans nobody else knows exist — led in the field by Daisy "Quake" Johnson, who generates seismic vibrations and has been Fury's protégée since she was a teenager Fury recruited out of the system. *Secret Warriors* is the era's spy-novel: layered conspiracies, ancient organizations, and Fury playing a game with a horizon of decades. It also plants Jonathan Hickman's first seeds in the main universe. Pay attention — this writer's habits (maps, councils, long games) will soon run everything.

primers.name: The Future Foundation & Valeria Richards
primers.text: Late in this era, Reed Richards does something uncharacteristic: he admits the way he works is broken, and founds the Future Foundation — a school of brilliant young minds (including his own children) tasked with solving everything. The standout is Valeria, Reed and Sue's daughter: a toddler whose intellect already rivals her father's and whose moral compass is worryingly Doom-flavored — she calls Victor "Uncle Doom," and means it. Hickman's FF run treats family as the universe's most powerful technology. Remember these kids; the road to Secret Wars runs through this household.

primers.name: Kid Loki
primers.text: Loki — Thor's brother, god of mischief, architect of half the Avengers' worst days — dies in Siege, and returns as a child with no memory of his crimes and a desperate wish not to become the monster everyone expects. *Journey Into Mystery* follows this boy-Loki working as Asgard's secret agent through the Fear Itself crisis, trying to save a world that hates him, one scheme at a time. It is widely considered one of the finest runs in this entire guide. The question it asks never resolves easily: can a story change its villain?

primers.name: The Worthy & The Serpent — CONCEPT
primers.text: Fear Itself introduces Cul Borson, the Serpent: Odin's forgotten brother, the original All-Father, a god of fear who grows stronger the more the world panics. His heralds, the Worthy, are heroes and villains possessed by ancient hammers that fall to Earth — each transformation erases the person into a engine of terror. The concept to hold onto is thematic: this event runs on fear itself as a weapon and a fuel, in a world still traumatized by a decade of escalating catastrophes. Even where the event stumbles, that idea — and Journey Into Mystery beside it — earns its place.

primers.name: The Phoenix Force — CONCEPT / ENTITY
primers.text: A cosmic entity of life, death, and rebirth — the sum of all psychic energy that ever will exist, manifesting as a great bird of fire. The Phoenix doesn't do small: it chooses hosts (Jean Grey, above all), burns worlds, and seeds new life from ash. As *Avengers vs. X-Men* opens, the Phoenix is returning to Earth while mutantkind sits at 198 souls — so the Avengers see an extinction-level threat inbound, and the X-Men see their species' only hope of rebirth. Both readings are defensible. That collision of two correct fears is the event.

primers.name: Apocalypse — En Sabah Nur
primers.text: The first mutant, born in ancient Egypt, immortal through Celestial technology and body-hopping, preaching one doctrine for five thousand years: only the strong survive, and weakness must be culled — including weak mutants. *Uncanny X-Force*, where this primer anchors, is built around his legacy: a black-ops team deciding what to do about his followers, his heirs, and the possibility of his return in an innocent form. Apocalypse is less a man than an ideology with a body count. The X-line will be arguing with that ideology — and occasionally agreeing with it — for the rest of the guide.

primers.name: Thor — Thor Odinson
primers.text: The God of Thunder, absent from the guide's opening years — Asgard fell in Ragnarok before this era began, and Thor was dead, or whatever gods are. He returns in 2007 to find his people reborn on Earth and a hero community shattered by Civil War in his absence. Thor is the Avengers' conscience from an older, more absolute age: his friendships with Tony Stark and Steve Rogers were forged before registration, secrets, and compromises, and he does not forgive the new world quickly. Watch his homecoming — it sets Asgard's whole trajectory.

primers.name: The Guardians of the Galaxy
primers.text: Born from the Annihilation wars: a proactive strike team founded by Star-Lord (Peter Quill, half-human space outlaw) to stop cosmic crises *before* they become annihilations. The roster is gloriously unlikely — Rocket Raccoon, a weaponized experiment with a genius for ordnance; Groot, a tree monarch of few words; Gamora, Thanos's adopted daughter and the deadliest woman in the galaxy; Drax, bred to kill Thanos; and others rotating through. They're soldiers with PTSD playing at being a team. This scrappy unit becomes the cosmic line's flagship for the rest of the guide. ---

primers.name: The Incursions & The Builders — CONCEPT
primers.text: The engine of Hickman's saga, explained as the characters learn it: parallel universes are colliding. When two Earths enter an "incursion," both universes die unless one Earth is destroyed first — an eight-hour countdown with no third option anyone can find. Behind the phenomenon stand ancient cosmic orders, the Builders foremost: the oldest species in creation, gardeners of universes, now returning to prune a multiverse they judge broken. Hold two ideas at once: the science-fiction scale, and the moral one — every solution to an incursion is somebody's genocide. The Illuminati are about to do arithmetic with worlds.

primers.name: Black Swan — Yabbat Ummon Tarru
primers.text: The woman who arrives with the first incursion: a pale, elegant priestess of the Black Swans, an order that serves the multiverse's destruction as a religion. She speaks in riddles, worships a power she calls Rabum Alal, and offers the Illuminati the only working knowledge anyone has of how incursions are survived — for a price she doesn't fully state. Black Swan is Hickman's herald of doom: courteous, terrifying, and never entirely trustworthy. When she smiles and says everything dies, believe the diagnosis, not necessarily the prescription.

primers.name: Miles Morales — Spider-Man (Earth-1610)
primers.text: In the Ultimate Universe — the modernized parallel line anchored as this guide's essential side track — a thirteen-year-old Brooklyn kid named Miles Morales is bitten by a stolen, genetically engineered spider days before that world's Peter Parker dies. Miles gains the classic powers plus camouflage and a venom sting, and absolutely no desire to be a hero — which is why his slow, guilty, brave decision to take up the mask lands so hard. Miles is the side track's heart, and his story does not stay contained in his own universe. Read him here, in full, before Secret Wars.

primers.name: The Maker — Ultimate Reed Richards
primers.text: The Ultimate Universe's Reed Richards took a different road: a younger, colder Reed whose genius curdled through catastrophe and betrayal into the conviction that humanity itself is the problem to be solved. As the Maker — masked, scarred, commanding a thousand years of accelerated evolution inside his City — he is what Reed Richards becomes without Sue, without family, without limits. He is introduced as the side track's great villain, but understand him as the guide's great *warning*: the distance between the two Reeds is circumstance, not intellect. The Maker survives things universes don't.

primers.name: Captain Marvel — Carol Danvers
primers.text: Air Force colonel, former Ms. Marvel, now claiming the name Captain Marvel — the legacy of the Kree hero Mar-Vell, whose DNA is fused with hers. Carol flies under her own power, absorbs and blasts energy, and is the Avengers' closest thing to a professional soldier-pilot: disciplined, funny, and quietly terrified of the brain lesion her powers are aggravating. DeConnick's run redefines her as an aspirational figure — the hero who keeps climbing because the fall isn't the point. Carol's stature only grows from here; she becomes one of the universe's central leaders, with all the burden that implies.

primers.name: Ms. Marvel — Kamala Khan
primers.text: A sixteen-year-old from Jersey City: Muslim, Pakistani-American, fanfiction writer, and the world's biggest Carol Danvers fan. When the Terrigen cloud (see primer 66) unlocks her Inhuman genes, Kamala gains shapeshifting "embiggening" powers — and immediately does what a fan would do: makes a costume and starts saving her neighborhood. Kamala is the most important new hero of this entire era — the proof that the Marvel Universe can still generate icons. Her Jersey City corner stays deliberately small and warm while the multiverse burns around it, and that contrast is the point.

primers.name: Jane Foster
primers.text: Thor's oldest human love, now Dr. Jane Foster — an accomplished physician and, when this primer anchors, a woman undergoing chemotherapy for breast cancer with characteristic refusal to be pitied. In Aaron's Thor saga Jane represents the mortal stake in gods' wars: she has spent a lifetime among Asgardians and loves them, but she measures them by human standards and finds them wanting. Keep her in mind through the Thor thread even when she seems peripheral. The question of what a good mortal does with a god's lifetime of failures hangs over everything she touches.

primers.name: Gorr the God Butcher
primers.text: A nameless alien whose children starved while his people begged indifferent gods for rain. Gorr found a weapon — All-Black, the Necrosword, a blade of living darkness that kills deities — and spent millennia methodically murdering every god in creation, building toward a finale of theological revenge. He is the opening villain of Jason Aaron's Thor epic and its philosophical engine: his accusation (gods who don't answer prayers deserve extinction) is one Thor can never fully refute. Gorr's shadow falls across the entire Thor thread, and his weapon's lineage matters far beyond him.

primers.name: The Superior Spider-Man — Otto Octavius
primers.text: Doctor Octopus — dying, brilliant, and out of second chances — executes the ultimate theft: he swaps his mind into Peter Parker's body and leaves Peter to die in his ruined one. Then, to everyone's horror, Otto decides to *keep* the role — to prove he can be a better Spider-Man than Parker ever was: more efficient, more ruthless, more "superior." The result is one of the era's boldest experiments: a villain sincerely trying to be a hero with a villain's toolkit and ego. Watch how the people who knew Peter respond. Something is wrong, and some of them can tell.

primers.name: Terrigen & The NuHumans — CONCEPT
primers.text: Terrigen is the Inhumans' sacred mutagen: in crystal or mist form it triggers transformation in anyone carrying Inhuman genes. For millennia, Attilan controlled it absolutely. *Inhumanity* breaks that control — Terrigen is released into Earth's atmosphere globally, and suddenly thousands of ordinary people worldwide (Kamala Khan among them) are cocooning and emerging with powers: a hidden diaspora Attilan never knew existed. The Inhumans go overnight from secret monarchy to a nation scrambling to gather its scattered people — just as mutantkind, still fragile, notices a new power rising. Remember the cloud. It becomes a casus belli.

primers.name: Moon Knight — Marc Spector
primers.text: A mercenary left for dead in Egypt, resurrected — or unhinged — beneath the statue of Khonshu, the moon god, whose fist of vengeance he claims to be. Marc Spector also lives as Steven Grant and Jake Lockley, personalities that may be disguises, dissociative identities, or something stranger; the comics refuse to settle it, and so does he. Ellis's six issues are the modern template: eerie, stylish, one-moonlit-mission-at-a-time stories in a white suit (so they see him coming). Moon Knight is Marvel's beautiful unreliable narrator. Trust his competence; question his cosmology.

primers.name: Uatu — The Watcher
primers.text: The Watchers are an ancient species sworn never to interfere, only to observe and record everything. Uatu, assigned to Earth, is the oath's most famous breaker — he has quietly helped humanity at crucial moments for decades, because he cares. He sees all of Earth's secrets: every sin, every hidden act, archived in his gaze. *Original Sin* begins with his murder and the theft of his eyes — which means every secret he ever witnessed is suddenly a weapon loose in the world. The event's fallout is less about the killer than about what pours out of the vault.

primers.name: Angela — Aldrif Odinsdottir
primers.text: A winged assassin from Heven, the Tenth Realm — a realm of angels erased from all memory and cut off from the World Tree by Odin in an ancient war. Angela was raised as Heven's finest hunter, mercenary to her core, ignorant of her own origins; Original Sin's revelations restore the Tenth Realm to reality and her true parentage becomes a live grenade in Asgardian politics. Angela matters as a walking consequence: proof that even gods' edited histories don't stay edited. Her arrival reopens the oldest wound in Odin's house.

primers.name: God Doom & Battleworld — CONCEPT
primers.text: When everything dies, this is what remains. Battleworld is a patchwork planet stitched from fragments of destroyed universes — medieval domains, monster-haunted wastes, and alternate Marvel timelines, each ruled by a baron under one absolute god-emperor: Doom, who did what the heroes could not and salvaged existence itself, then rewrote reality with himself at its center and his enemies' lives rearranged to suit him. *Secret Wars* is the guide's hinge — the end of the old multiverse and the seedbed of the new one. Read it as both finale and creation myth: everything after happens in a universe Doom, in some sense, made. ---

primers.name: Kobik & Pleasant Hill — CONCEPT
primers.text: S.H.I.E.L.D.'s darkest experiment: fragments of Cosmic Cube — reality-warping energy — that unexpectedly coalesced into a sentient child. Kobik is a four-year-old girl who can rewrite reality on a whim, and S.H.I.E.L.D. used her to build Pleasant Hill: a prison disguised as a perfect small town, where supervillains are brainwashed into believing they're barbers and bakers. It is exactly as ethical as it sounds. Everything about *Standoff!* and the Secret Empire saga grows from this one decision: a weaponized child-god, raised on stories told by the wrong people. Watch who tells Kobik her stories.

primers.name: Captain America — Sam Wilson
primers.text: Sam Wilson — the Falcon, Steve Rogers' partner of decades, a social worker from Harlem who flies on a winged harness and talks to birds — took up the shield when Steve lost the Super-Soldier Serum and aged into an old man. His Captain America is immediately political in a way Steve's couldn't avoid being: a Black man carrying the flag through a polarized America, targeted by pundits, corporations, and the government he serves. Sam's tenure is the era's clearest statement that the shield is an argument about the country. His friendship with Steve is the saga's load-bearing wall — which is precisely why the coming event aims at it.

primers.name: The New Steve Rogers — READ WITH CARE
primers.text: At the end of *Standoff!*, Kobik restores Steve Rogers to his young, super-soldier prime — the icon is back, and the whole universe exhales. Then you read *Captain America: Steve Rogers* #1, and its final page lands like a hammer: something about this Steve is profoundly, historically *wrong*, in a way that reaches back to his childhood in the 1930s. This primer will not say more; the series itself explains, carefully and at length, and the explanation is the Secret Empire saga's whole subject. What you need going in: this is not a trick, a clone, or a dream — the story insists on that, and means it.

primers.name: The Vision & His Family
primers.text: The Avengers' android: a synthezoid with solar-powered density control, built from villainous origins into one of the team's most quietly human members. Tom King's *Vision* finds him attempting the final step of assimilation — he has built himself a synthezoid wife, Virginia, and twin children, and moved them to a Virginia suburb to simply *be* a family. It goes the way Greek tragedy goes. This twelve-issue series is the most acclaimed single book of the era and needs no continuity beyond this primer: a machine trying to be a man, and the arithmetic of what that costs everyone in the house.

primers.name: Riri Williams — Ironheart
primers.text: A fifteen-year-old MIT engineering prodigy from Chicago who reverse-engineered Iron Man armor in her dorm room from scavenged parts. Tony Stark, rather than suing her, becomes her mentor — and when Tony falls in Civil War II, Riri steps into the sky in armor of her own design as Ironheart. She represents the era's generational bet: the future of the Marvel Universe belongs to brilliant kids who grew up watching the Avengers and decided the job was theirs to inherit. Her grief (she lost her best friend and stepfather to gun violence) is her engine, not her ornament.

primers.name: The Champions — CONCEPT / TEAM
primers.text: After Civil War II, the Marvel Universe's teenage heroes — Miles Morales, Kamala Khan, the young Nova (Sam Alexander), Amadeus Cho's Hulk, Viv Vision, and a time-displaced young Cyclops — walk out on the adult Avengers in disgust. Their founding argument: the grown-ups keep breaking the world and calling it necessary; heroes should save people, not win wars, and should be accountable for collateral damage. The Champions are the era's conscience in teenage form. Their importance is cumulative — this generation is being positioned, book by book, as the universe's future leadership. Watch them grow up; the guide is long, and so is their arc.

primers.name: The Mighty Thor — The New Goddess of Thunder
primers.text: After *Original Sin*, Thor Odinson can no longer lift Mjolnir — a whisper from Nick Fury made him unworthy, and the hammer sat on the Moon until a woman picked it up. The new Thor's identity is a genuine mystery the series guards: she is dying (the transformation is tangled up with a mortal illness), Asgard's establishment calls her a thief and a usurper, and Malekith's war of conquest is burning the Ten Realms while the gods argue. She is, by wide agreement, worthy. The run built around her is the back half of Aaron's Thor epic — treat the mystery as the story, not a puzzle to beat.

primers.name: Malekith the Accursed
primers.text: The dark elf king of Svartalfheim: a sadistic sorcerer-warrior who survived his own people's massacre and turned grievance into a career of conquest. Across Aaron's Thor saga, Malekith assembles a council of the realms' worst powers — fire demons, frost giants, angels, and corporate Roxxon — and methodically conquers the Ten Realms one by one while the Thors bleed to slow him. He is the Thor thread's true main villain, and the guide tracks his conquest tally like a sports table for years. When *War of the Realms* finally arrives, it's the bill for everything in this primer.

primers.name: Venom — Eddie Brock
primers.text: A disgraced journalist bonded to an alien symbiote — a living black suit that amplifies his strength, mimics Spider-Man's powers, and shares his hatreds. For decades Venom was a monster with a code: lethal protector of innocents, eater of brains in his worse years. Donny Cates's run, where this primer anchors, reframes everything: the symbiotes (the Klyntar) have a god, a history, and a purpose Eddie never knew, and Eddie has a personal stake — family — he never expected. Brock's evolution from villain to one of the universe's most important figures starts here. It is not a short road.

primers.name: Knull — God of the Symbiotes
primers.text: Before light, there was the abyss — and Knull was its king. An elder god who existed before the universe's creation, forger of the first symbiote from living darkness, and creator of the Klyntar as a hive-army to extinguish the light of the cosmos. The symbiotes eventually imprisoned him at the heart of their world; everything in Venom's mythology is downstream of that rebellion and his slow, patient stirring. Cates builds Knull the way the guide loves: as a rumor, a symbol (the spiral), a red dragon in old stories — long before he arrives in person. When he does, it's an event. You have been warned the way Eddie was: in pieces.

primers.name: Carnage — Cletus Kasady
primers.text: When Venom's symbiote reproduced, its offspring bonded to Eddie's cellmate: Cletus Kasady, a remorseless serial killer whose philosophy is that life is chaos and murder is honesty. The result, Carnage, is stronger than Venom and Spider-Man combined and utterly without Venom's code — a red nightmare that treats massacres as self-expression. By *Absolute Carnage*, the Cates saga has given Kasady a horrifying new purpose connected to Knull and the codex fragments every symbiote host carries. He is the Venom line's purest horror element: no redemption arc, no tragic excuse. Just appetite, escalating.

primers.name: The Immortal Hulk — The Green Door & Hulk's Personas — CONCEPT
primers.text: Al Ewing's horror masterpiece begins from a simple observation: Bruce Banner can die, but at night, the Hulk comes back — the Hulk has *always* come back. This run treats Hulk's transformations as a system of distinct personas (the childlike Savage Hulk, the cunning Joe Fixit, and worse things deeper down) governed by rules, haunted by a metaphysical "Green Door" between life and death that gamma keeps opening. It's a horror comic about fathers, abuse, and the devil you carry. Fifty issues, complete, and arguably the single best run in this entire guide. Read it slowly, at night.

primers.name: Old Man Logan — SIDE TRACK S1
primers.text: A side-track callout, anchored here: in a possible future where the villains finally organized and won, an elderly Wolverine — broken by a night he refuses to discuss — lives as a pacifist farmer in a wasteland America carved up among tyrants. The original story is one of the most famous Wolverine tales ever told; this ongoing series imports that Logan into the main universe's present, a traumatized old soldier among younger versions of his dead friends. He's a visitor in the main order, not a resident: read his track for texture, and because his guilt is a masterclass in Logan.

primers.name: Spider-Gwen — Gwen Stacy of Earth-65 — SIDE TRACK S2
primers.text: On Earth-65, the spider bit Gwen Stacy instead of Peter Parker — and Peter, desperate to be special like her, became this world's Lizard and died in her arms, making her a fugitive blamed for her best friend's death. Gwen is a drummer, a wisecracking Spider-Woman in a hood, and the breakout star of the Spider-Verse concept. Her series is a side track — her own universe, her own supporting cast (including a villainous Matt Murdock) — but she crosses into the main universe often enough that the guide anchors her here, at her launch. Alternate-earth, full heart.

primers.name: Krakoa — The Mutant Nation — CONCEPT
primers.text: Krakoa is a living island — a mutant organism the size of a country — and, as of *House of X*, it is also a sovereign nation: mutantkind's first true homeland, recognized by the world's governments in exchange for miracle drugs that extend human life. Anyone with the X-gene can walk through its gateways from anywhere on Earth. Xavier's pitch to his people is total: no more hiding, no more assimilation — mutant culture, mutant law, mutant future, on an island that is itself a mutant. Everything in the X-line from 2019 onward is Krakoan politics, economics, faith, and war. This is the biggest status-quo shift in the guide since M-Day — and note the symmetry: Decimation nearly ended the species; Krakoa is the answer built from that trauma.

primers.name: Moira MacTaggert — Moira's Lives — CONCEPT
primers.text: Dr. Moira MacTaggert was, for forty years of comics, the X-Men's human ally: a geneticist, Xavier's old flame, a Nobel winner who ran a research center on Muir Island. *House of X* reveals she was never human at all. Moira's mutant power is reincarnation with perfect memory: each time she dies, she restarts her own life in the womb, remembering everything — and she has lived nine full lives of mutant history, trying every strategy (Xavier's dream, Magneto's war, Apocalypse's crusade, and worse) and watching all of them end the same way: machines, and extinction. Krakoa is her tenth life's final, combined plan. She is the secret architect of the entire modern X-era — and a woman who has watched everyone she loves die nine times. Hold onto that.

primers.name: The Five & The Resurrection Protocols — CONCEPT
primers.text: Krakoa's miracle, and the mechanism that changes the stakes of every X-story after it: five mutants whose powers combine into a circuit — Goldballs' eggs, Proteus's reality-warping, Elixir's biokinesis, Tempus's time control, and Hope Summers' power-mimicry binding them — can grow clone bodies into which a dead mutant's recorded mind (archived by Cerebro) is restored. Death, for mutants, is now an inconvenience. The Resurrection Protocols are why Krakoa can be so bold, and the questions they raise — is the restored person the same person? what happens to a culture without death? — power half the era's best stories. Note Hope's place in the circuit: the messiah became infrastructure.

primers.name: Mutant Circuits — CONCEPT
primers.text: On Krakoa, mutant powers are treated as technology: a "circuit" is a team of mutants whose abilities interlock into something none could do alone — resurrection is simply the most famous circuit. Teleporters plus weather-workers terraform; telepaths plus technopaths build information networks; the Great Ring of Arakko (see primer 120) fights wars as living systems. This concept is the Krakoa era's design philosophy: mutantkind's superiority isn't individual power, it's *combination* — a people who were hunted alone choosing to be unkillable together. When a story says "the circuit," it means mutants deliberately engineering miracles as a culture.

primers.name: Orchis & Nimrod — CONCEPT
primers.text: Moira's nine lives all end the same way, and Orchis is how the tenth tries to: a black-budget alliance of every anti-mutant power on Earth — ex-S.H.I.E.L.D., ex-Hydra, A.I.M., human-supremacist money and science — building toward one weapon: Nimrod, the ultimate Sentinel, a self-improving machine intelligence that no mutant force has ever beaten in any timeline Moira lived. Orchis works from a station orbiting the sun and waits, patiently, for mutantkind to make a mistake. They are the Krakoa era's true antagonist: not a villain, but an extinction process with an org chart. Every year of the era, the Orchis countdown ticks. ---

primers.name: The Quiet Council — CONCEPT / TEAM
primers.text: Krakoa's government: twelve seats around a table in the island's heart, divided into seasonal blocs — Xavier, Magneto, and Apocalypse among them; Emma Frost and Storm holding commercial and moral weight; and, from the start, seats filled by people like Mystique and Mister Sinister, because Krakoa's founding bargain was amnesty for *every* mutant, monster included. The Council writes the nation's three laws (make more mutants; murder no man; respect the land) and breaks its own spirit constantly. *Immortal X-Men* turns their closed-door sessions into the era's political thriller. Watch the empty seats, the bargains, and who is always absent when votes are taken — Krakoa's fate is decided in this room.

primers.name: Saturnyne & Otherworld — CONCEPT
primers.text: Otherworld is the nexus realm of the multiverse — a fantasy patchwork of kingdoms sitting at the junction of all realities, ruled from the Starlight Citadel by Opal Luna Saturnyne, the Omniversal Majestrix: a serene, ruthless bureaucrat-goddess who treats cosmic order as her personal filing system and the Captain Britain Corps as her police. The Krakoa era entangles mutantkind with Otherworld through Excalibur and the tournament of *X of Swords*, because Apocalypse's oldest secrets are buried there. Saturnyne never loses her composure or, somehow, an argument. When she smiles at the X-Men, check what she's just taken from them.

primers.name: Arakko — The Lost Island & Its People
primers.text: Thousands of years ago, Krakoa was one island — until it split in two. The other half, Arakko, was carried into a demon dimension to hold back an endless invasion, and its mutants spent millennia in a war that never paused, evolving a culture where weakness is literally unspeakable and every adult is a veteran. *X of Swords* is the story of the two islands' reunion — and of two peoples who are technically one nation and share almost nothing else. Arakko's warriors (and their Great Ring of omega-level living weapons) become central to the era's cosmic half. Remember: Krakoans fear death now that they've beaten it; Arakki never had that luxury.

primers.name: Mister Sinister — Nathaniel Essex
primers.text: A Victorian geneticist who traded his humanity to Apocalypse for immortality and has spent 150 years cloning, scheming, and collecting mutant DNA — in the Krakoa era, his gene banks are literally the archive resurrection runs on, which buys this flamboyant, cape-swishing monster a seat on the Quiet Council. Gillen's Sinister is the era's great unreliable narrator: camp, brilliant, and running schemes inside schemes, several of which involve copies of himself he doesn't tell the others about. Every Sinister scene is a magic trick — watch the hand he wants you to watch, then assume the other one did something worse. *Sins of Sinister* is what happens when one of his tricks finally works completely.

primers.name: Mother Righteous
primers.text: A red-skinned, four-armed sorceress-thief who trades in faith: she collects belief the way banks collect interest, offering miracles and gratitude-powered magic across the margins of the Krakoa era. She drifts through *Legion of X* and the era's magical corners as a seemingly minor player — a fixer, a tempter, a face in the crowd of every crisis. Minor players with unexplained power and perfect timing deserve suspicion in this era above all others; the Krakoa saga is built out of long-hidden architects. When Mother Righteous offers thanks, ask what she's banking.

primers.name: The Eternals & The Progenitor — CONCEPT
primers.text: The Eternals are an immortal, unchanging race created by the Celestials — cosmic giants who seeded life across the universe — to protect Earth from their monstrous counterparts, the Deviants. Their society runs on three Principles enforced by a planetary Machine: correct excess deviation, protect the Celestials' garden, and — the horror at their core — every Eternal resurrection is powered by a human death, a tithe they've paid in ignorance for a million years. *Judgment Day* wakes a dead Celestial, the Progenitor, who announces it will judge every soul on Earth, hero and villain and bystander, within twenty-four hours. The Eternals' internal schism over mutantkind (are mutants "excess deviation"?) lights the fuse; the Progenitor is the clock.

primers.name: Druig — Prime Eternal (Acting)
primers.text: When Judgment Day opens, the Eternals' throne is held by Druig — a schemer of the old school: smooth, patient, and willing to burn any principle to keep power, in a species whose entire tragedy is that they *cannot* abandon theirs. It is Druig who points the Eternals' war machine at Krakoa, for reasons that mix genuine doctrine with personal ambition in proportions he himself may not know. He makes a perfect era villain because he's not wrong about everything: his people really are dying of their purpose, and his solution is merely monstrous. Watch the gap between what Druig says the Principles demand and what Druig wants.

primers.name: Marc Spector's New Mission — The Midnight Mission (MacKay Era)
primers.text: By the time Jed MacKay's run opens, Moon Knight has done something new: opened a storefront. The Midnight Mission is a neighborhood office in New York where anyone can walk in and ask the protection of Khonshu's fist — and Marc Spector, suit and mask immaculate, keeps office hours like a therapist with a body count. This run assembles a small, beloved supporting cast, rebuilds Marc's world from street level, and treats his fractured mind with unusual tenderness — while vampires, rival fists, and old sins queue outside. The MacKay web (Moon Knight, Strange, Avengers) is the modern era's spine; it starts in this little office, with a man trying to be a priest of a violent god.

primers.name: Clea Strange — Sorcerer Supreme
primers.text: Clea is a warlord-princess of the Dark Dimension — niece of the dread Dormammu, a sorceress of Faltine fire raised in a realm her family rules by terror — and Stephen Strange's wife, exiled to Earth and long his partner in magic. The MacKay *Strange* sequence begins from loss: with Stephen dead (the *Death of Doctor Strange* is its prerequisite), the mantle of Sorcerer Supreme passes to Clea, who wages a one-woman war to resurrect her husband while defending a dimension that isn't hers by birth. She is more powerful and far less merciful than Stephen. Earth's magical community has to adjust; so does death.

primers.name: Kang the Conqueror — MacKay Avengers Anchor
primers.text: Kang has haunted the Avengers since the beginning — a time-traveling warlord from the far future, armed with all of history as an arsenal, who conquers eras the way other men collect art (and who first appeared in this guide as the Young Avengers' Iron Lad mystery, Era 02 §5B.6). In MacKay's *Avengers*, something unprecedented happens: Kang comes to the Avengers *for help*, dying, with a warning — events called the Tribulation Events are coming, a "Missing Moment" has been stolen from time, and powers called the Ashen Combine are moving. Kang as terrified informant reframes him completely: when the man who has seen all of time is scared, the Avengers listen. So should you.

primers.name: Varnae & The Vampire Nation — CONCEPT
primers.text: Vampires in the Marvel Universe descend from Varnae, the first vampire — an Atlantean sorcerer transformed in ancient times, whose bloodline curse passed down through Dracula himself. For centuries Marvel's vampires were scattered, hunted, or corralled into a fragile nation-state under Dracula's rule. *Blood Hunt* is what happens when that patience ends: a coordinated, global vampire uprising engineered by a hidden hand, exploiting a darkness that falls over the whole Earth at once. The event is a horror-war story, and its architect's identity is one of its central reveals — go in knowing only that the vampires have never, ever been this organized, and ask yourself why now.

primers.name: Doom Ascendant — One World Under Doom — CONCEPT
primers.text: By 2025, Victor von Doom has accumulated the one thing he always lacked: the Sorcerer Supreme's mantle (taken in *Blood Hunt*'s fallout), added to his armor, his nation, and his will. Then he does the most Doom thing imaginable — he doesn't invade the world. He *saves* it, publicly, repeatedly, undeniably: ending wars, fixing crises, offering every nation prosperity under Latverian administration, until the world's governments ask him to rule. *One World Under Doom* asks the question Doom has posed since 1961 with the volume turned up: if the tyrant is genuinely better at this than the heroes and democracies — what exactly is the argument against him? Reed Richards has to find one. It's the best Doom story in decades, and it only works because you met him in primer 18.

primers.name: The Shi'ar Empire & Imperial — CONCEPT
primers.text: The Shi'ar are the oldest and most militarized of the great space empires: an avian-descended civilization ruled from the throneworld Chandilar, enforcers of galactic order through the Imperial Guard — a legion of super-powered champions led by Gladiator, a mohawked titan whose strength literally scales with his confidence. *Imperial*, Hickman's return to the cosmic board, is a story of thrones: assassinations, succession crises, and the great powers (Shi'ar, Kree-Skrull alliance, Wakanda's intergalactic empire, Nova's reborn corps) recalculating what the galaxy is after Krakoa and Judgment Day rearranged the pieces. If the Annihilation saga (primers 37–41) was cosmic war, *Imperial* is cosmic *statecraft* — same players, colder weapons.

primers.name: Doug Ramsey — Revelation
primers.text: Long-time readers know Doug Ramsey as Cypher: the New Mutants' gentle linguist, a mutant whose power is understanding any language, once the X-Men's most famously "useless" member in a fight and one of its most beloved souls. In the post-Krakoa era Doug has become something else — the Heir of Apocalypse, chosen in the *Heir of Apocalypse* succession contest, carrying a portion of En Sabah Nur's power and his doctrine's terrible logic. *Age of Revelation* shows a possible future built in his image: a mutant utopia spreading across America, enforced absolutely. The horror of it is that the architect is Doug — the kindest mutant — reasoning his way, step by defensible step, to Apocalypse's conclusions. Watch the reasoning, not just the result.

primers.name: The New Ultimate Universe — Earth-6160 — SIDE TRACK S
primers.text: The essential side track of the modern era, anchored where it launches: the Maker (primer 60) escaped the end of his own universe and found a new one — a world he could reach *before* its heroes happened, and quietly edit: stealing destinies, delaying origins, ruling from behind a council of proxies for decades. Earth-6160 is that world: a Marvel Universe with its history stolen, where a middle-aged Peter Parker only now receives his powers, where the Ultimates are a resistance network with a countdown clock, and where every title is racing the Maker's return. It is deliberately readable as its own complete saga alongside the main order — and the guide's suggested windows (notably: binge it after Blood Hunt) are in Era 06 Part S. When the Maker's countdown ends, it ends for both tracks.

primers.name: The Maker's Council & The Children of Tomorrow — 6160 CONCEPT
primers.text: How do you rule a world whose heroes you prevented? The Maker governs Earth-6160 through a shadow council of regional powers — among them a Hulk who rules through weaponized serenity, a Captain America who never was, and Emmanuel da Costa's solar empire — each granted a territory in exchange for keeping history on rails. His original instrument, the Children of Tomorrow, were his accelerated-evolution army from the City: post-human, beautiful, and expendable. The 6160 track's tension is structural: a world designed by a villain, populated by people who don't know their lives were edited. Every hero who emerges there is a glitch in the Maker's design — which is why he counts glitches so carefully. ---

primers.name: The Stepford Cuckoos
primers.text: Five identical blonde telepaths — Celeste, Esme, Irma, Phoebe, and Sophie — who arrive at Xavier's school as Emma Frost's prize students and operate as a single hive mind: five bodies, one cold, precise, faintly contemptuous personality, finishing each other's sentences in chorus. Where Emma performs warmth as strategy, her Cuckoos don't bother performing at all. They are the student body's aristocracy and its early-warning system, loyal to Emma and to each other before any cause. A hive mind is a formidable thing — until one of the five starts thinking something the others don't share.

primers.name: Laura Kinney — X-23
primers.text: A teenage girl found among New York's homeless mutant runaways: two claws in each hand, one in each foot, a healing factor that never switches off — Wolverine's exact signature in a kid who barely speaks. *NYX* tells you almost nothing about where she came from, and the silence is the point: Laura Kinney — "X-23" in files she has never seen — is a person whose past was done *to* her, by people who built her as a weapon. The guide excavates how she was made later, in her own books. Start here, with what it costs a weapon to try being a person.

primers.name: The Red Skull — Johann Schmidt
primers.text: A hotel bellboy Hitler personally molded into the Nazi ideal: Captain America's oldest enemy, his face the ideology made literal. The Skull has died before; it didn't take. As Brubaker's run opens he is back in play — his consciousness lodged inside the mind of Russian oligarch Aleksander Lukin, two monsters sharing one body and one long patience. The Skull doesn't want to beat Steve Rogers in a fight. He wants to rot everything Steve stands for, slowly, from inside the century that replaced the war. Every Captain America story in this era is partly his.

primers.name: Daken
primers.text: Wolverine has a son. Logan never knew: the boy was cut from his murdered mother's womb in 1946, raised in secrecy, and taught one lesson above all others — his absent father is the reason for every bad thing in his life. Daken (the name is an insult in two languages) carries his father's claws and healing, plus a pheromone gift for bending a room's emotions, and none of Logan's hard-won restraint. *Origins* seeds him in shadow; the full reveal lands just past this era. When father and son finally meet, it will not be a reunion. Someone spent sixty years making sure of that.

primers.name: Maria Hill
primers.text: When Nick Fury vanishes, his chair doesn't go to a legend — it goes to Maria Hill, a career S.H.I.E.L.D. soldier with no mystique, no serum, and a by-the-book streak a mile wide. As *Civil War* opens she is the acting director enforcing registration, and she moves to arrest Captain America before the law she's enforcing has even passed. Hill is what the security state looks like without a spymaster's romance: competent, rigid, certain the file is right. Track her across the guide — her stands and her compromises map exactly how far the institution drifts in Fury's absence.

primers.name: Exodus
primers.text: Bennet du Paris was a twelfth-century crusader before Apocalypse remade him — an immensely powerful telekinetic who has spent eight centuries as a true believer, transferring his devotion from cause to cause without ever losing its intensity. In the Messiah era he leads the Acolytes, mutantkind's most zealous faithful, and he comes for the first mutant baby as a worshipper, not a strategist: Hope Summers is his religion made flesh. Exodus is the X-line's holy warrior — frightening not because he is cruel, but because he is sincere, and because a man who has buried eight centuries of certainties will always find a new one.

primers.name: Amadeus Cho
primers.text: A Korean-American teenager whose hypertrophied brain runs physics like a video game — trajectories, probabilities, outcomes, computed in real time — which, by his own cheerful ranking, makes him about the seventh smartest person on Earth. He enters the guide on the Hulk's side of World War Hulk, insisting the math proves Banner never kills the innocent, then stays on as Hercules' sidekick and conscience. Cho is the era's optimism engine: the kid who believes every monster in this guide is one correct calculation away from being saved. The guide will test that belief for twenty years.

primers.name: Abigail Brand
primers.text: Abigail Brand commands S.W.O.R.D., the orbital agency whose whole job is the day the aliens invade — which, in this era, is most days. Half-alien herself (she keeps the green hair; the rest she files down), Brand is the most pragmatic person in any room she enters: she frees Reed Richards mid-invasion, treats diplomacy as a targeting problem, and answers to results rather than to anyone's chain of command. The X-Men find her useful and unnerving in equal measure. Keep that ratio in mind. Brand recurs across the entire guide, and her loyalties are never as simple as her competence.

primers.name: The Hood — Parker Robbins
primers.text: Parker Robbins was a nobody — a small-time crook with a sick mother and a baby coming — until he shot a demon in an empty warehouse and took its cloak and boots. The cloak lets him walk on air and vanish; it also comes from somewhere infernal, and the price schedule is deliberately unclear. Robbins' real talent isn't power, it's organization: while the heroes tear themselves apart, he builds the underworld its first syndicate — supervillains with a union, a pension plan, and a boss. By Dark Reign he sits at Osborn's own table. The Hood is this era's proof that vacuums get filled from below.

primers.name: Legion — David Haller
primers.text: David Haller is Professor Xavier's son, and the strongest argument in the guide that power and damage scale together. David is an omega-level mutant whose fractured mind houses hundreds of distinct personalities — and each personality holds a different power, so whichever one is driving decides what David can do, and David is not always driving. He returns to the X-Men's world in the run-up to *Second Coming* as a catastrophe other people manage, not a person anyone thinks to ask. That is the tragedy the later books inherit: the most powerful mutant alive is a crowd, and the boy in the middle just wants a turn at his own life.

primers.name: Baron Zemo — Helmut Zemo
primers.anchor_series: Captain America — the Trial of Captain America setup
primers.text: Helmut Zemo, thirteenth Baron Zemo: son of the Nazi scientist whose death Captain America helped cause, his own face melted into his mask by his father's chemicals. Zemo has led the Masters of Evil and once ran the Thunderbolts as a long con in a hero's costume — his lifelong thesis being that the world is safer *ruled*, preferably by him.
